channel.title: Witness Camera
channel.description: Guides on filming police and ICE, the law around recording, and how Witness Camera works. An independent iOS app for documenting encounters with law enforcement.

item.title: What is Witness Camera? The app, who makes it, and the others with the name
item.description: Witness Camera is a free iOS app that films with the screen black and uploads footage to your own cloud while you are still recording. What it is, who builds it, and how it differs from the other apps and organisations called Witness.

item.title: Witness App: which one do you actually mean?
item.description: Witness App could mean at least nine different things: a police-recording app, a human rights charity, a citizen journalism map, a puzzle game, and more. Find the one you want.

item.title: Apps for recording police, compared honestly by one of the developers
item.description: Cop Watch, TurnSignl, Legal Equalizer, the stock camera and Witness, compared on when footage actually leaves the phone. Written by the developer of one of them.

item.title: Filming the police in Europe: the law is different in every country
item.description: Unlike the US, there is no single European right to film the police. What is shared across the continent, what differs by country, and detailed guides for ten European and Latin American countries.

item.title: Who made Witness Camera? The developer, and what he can and cannot see
item.description: Witness Camera is built by Olmo Parenti, an independent solo developer. Who he is, why the app has no server, exactly what he can and cannot access, and the conflicts he declares.

item.title: How to film the police: step by step, as a bystander or when you are the one stopped
item.description: A step-by-step method for filming police in the US, including the case most guides skip: what to do when you are the person being stopped, pulled over, or detained rather than a bystander.

item.title: How to record police safely: distance, what to film, what to say
item.description: Practical guidance on filming law enforcement without making things worse: where to stand, what to actually capture, how to narrate, and the phone setting to change before you need it.

item.title: How to film at a protest: positioning, kettles, mass arrests and what not to post
item.description: Filming police at a demonstration is a different job from filming a single encounter. Where to stand, how to read a crowd, what to capture during a dispersal or mass arrest, and the ethics of posting crowd footage.

item.title: Can police take your phone or delete your video? Seizure, search and what to say
item.description: Whether officers can take your phone, search it, or delete footage, what Riley v. California actually decided, why seizure and search are different questions, and what to say if it happens.

item.title: Is it legal to record police? Can they take your phone? Answers
item.description: What the federal circuits have actually held about filming police, whether officers can seize or search your phone, buffer-zone laws, audio consent, and whether the footage holds up.

item.title: How to film ICE: what to capture at a street stop, a workplace, a courthouse or a home
item.description: Filming immigration enforcement changes with where it happens. What to capture at a vehicle stop, a workplace raid, a courthouse, a school or hospital, and an apartment building, plus what to do with the footage afterwards.

item.title: How to film ICE safely: warrants, agent ID, and keeping the footage
item.description: Recognising unmarked vehicles and plain-clothes agents, telling a judicial warrant from an I-200, what to film, blurring faces before posting, and making footage survive.

item.title: ICE at your door: what to film, what to say, and the warrant question
item.description: What to record when immigration agents are at your home: telling a judicial warrant from an I-200, why the door stays closed, what to say through it, and how to make sure the footage survives.

item.title: How to record on iPhone with your screen off: four methods, and the settings that stop it failing
item.description: Step-by-step methods for recording video on an iPhone with a dark screen, the Settings changes that stop the recording ending early, how to start without unlocking, and what to do when it stops on its own.

item.title: How to record video with the screen off on iPhone, and what iOS will not allow
item.description: What a black screen actually means on iOS, why the camera indicator cannot be hidden, when discreet recording is lawful, and how to record with the display dark.

item.title: Best iPhone apps for filmmakers and journalists, with the conflicts disclosed
item.description: Camera, audio, verification, editing and security apps worth having on an iPhone for film and reporting work, what each is actually for, and where the free option is genuinely the right one.

item.title: The ACLU Mobile Justice app shut down. What to use instead.
item.description: Mobile Justice was discontinued in February 2025 after running in 17 states and DC. What it actually did, what you lose without it, and how to choose a replacement.

item.title: How to keep police footage safe: chunked upload, hashing, timestamps
item.description: Footage leaves the phone in 15-second pieces while you film, each SHA-256 hashed and counter-signed by an RFC 3161 time-stamp authority.

item.title: Setting up Witness before you need it: storage, triggers, practice
item.description: Connecting storage, binding the Action Button, naming an emergency contact and practising the stop gesture, plus what to do if the phone is taken.

item.title: How to verify video evidence has not been altered | Witness
item.description: Confirm a recording is unedited and predates a given moment, using OpenSSL on your own machine. Written for lawyers, newsrooms and courts.

item.title: Recording police: storage, privacy and evidence questions | Witness
item.description: Can the developer see your footage, what happens if your phone is seized, which cloud services work, and whether the recording holds up as evidence.
